topics.desc: An atom is the basic unit of a chemical element. It has a nucleus of protons and neutrons, with electrons around the nucleus. The number of protons, called the atomic number, identifies the element.

topics.title: Molecules
topics.desc: A molecule is two or more atoms bonded together. The atoms can be the same, as in O₂, or different, as in water, H₂O. The chemical formula tells you which atoms are in the molecule and how many of each.

topics.title: The periodic table
topics.desc: The periodic table organizes elements by atomic number. Rows are called periods and columns are called groups. Elements in the same group often have similar chemical properties, such as the noble gases in the far-right column.

topics.title: States of matter
topics.desc: The common states of matter are solid, liquid and gas. In a solid, particles are packed in a fixed shape. In a liquid they flow and take the shape of the container. In a gas they spread out to fill the available space. Heat or pressure can change the state.

topics.title: Density
topics.desc: Density is mass divided by volume. A material with higher density has more mass in the same amount of space. That is why a steel bolt sinks in water while a larger piece of wood can float: steel’s density is greater than water’s, and most wood is less dense than water.

topics.title: Acids and bases
topics.desc: Acids and bases are opposite kinds of substances in water. Acids increase hydrogen ion concentration and often taste sour, such as lemon juice. Bases decrease that concentration or increase hydroxide, and many feel slippery, such as soap. They can neutralize each other.

topics.title: pH
topics.desc: pH is a scale that usually runs from 0 to 14 and measures how acidic or basic a water solution is. 7 is neutral, like pure water. Numbers below 7 are acidic and numbers above 7 are basic. Each step of 1 is a tenfold change in acidity.

topics.title: Chemical versus physical change
topics.desc: A physical change alters form but not the substance itself, such as melting ice or tearing paper. A chemical change makes a new substance, such as burning wood or baking a cake. Clues can include a new color, gas, temperature change or unexpected solid, though those clues are not proof by themselves.

topics.title: Animal and plant cells
topics.desc: Both animal and plant cells have a nucleus, cytoplasm and a cell membrane. Plant cells also have a cell wall and usually chloroplasts for photosynthesis, and they often have a large central vacuole. Animal cells do not have a cell wall or chloroplasts.

topics.title: DNA
topics.desc: DNA is the molecule in cells that carries genetic instructions. It is shaped like a double helix, a twisted ladder, with paired bases: A with T, and C with G. Those instructions help determine how an organism grows and how its cells work.

topics.title: Food chains
topics.desc: A food chain shows how energy moves from one living thing to another. It often starts with a producer, such as a plant, that makes its own food. A consumer eats plants or other animals, and a decomposer breaks down dead material. Arrows point toward the eater, the direction energy flows.

topics.title: Ecosystems
topics.desc: An ecosystem is a community of living things plus the nonliving parts of their environment, such as water, soil, air and climate. A change in one part, like a drought or the loss of a species, can affect many other parts.

topics.title: The water cycle
topics.desc: The water cycle is the movement of water between Earth’s surface and the atmosphere. Water evaporates, condenses into clouds, and falls as precipitation. It can then flow as runoff, soak into the ground, or evaporate again.

topics.title: The solar system
topics.desc: The solar system is the Sun and everything that orbits it, including eight planets, moons, asteroids and comets. The four inner planets are rocky. The four outer planets are much larger and are mostly gas and ice. Gravity from the Sun keeps the planets in orbit.

topics.title: Solar and lunar eclipses
topics.desc: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth and the Moon’s shadow falls on Earth. A lunar eclipse happens when Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon and Earth’s shadow falls on the Moon. They do not occur every month because the Moon’s orbit is tilted.

topics.title: Plate tectonics
topics.desc: Earth’s outer shell is broken into large plates that move slowly over the mantle. Where plates meet they can pull apart, collide, or slide past each other. That movement helps explain earthquakes, many volcanoes, and the building of mountain ranges.

topics.title: Earthquakes
topics.desc: An earthquake is the shaking caused when rocks along a fault suddenly slip and release energy as seismic waves. Most earthquakes occur near tectonic plate boundaries. During shaking, drop to the ground, take cover under sturdy furniture, and hold on until it stops.

topics.title: Volcanoes
topics.desc: A volcano is an opening where molten rock, ash and gas can reach the surface. Most volcanoes form near plate boundaries, especially where a plate sinks or where plates pull apart. Magma is molten rock underground; once it reaches the surface it is called lava.

topics.title: Fossils
topics.desc: Fossils are remains or traces of past life, such as bones, shells, footprints or leaf impressions, preserved in rock. They form more often when an organism is buried quickly and hard parts are slowly replaced or left as an imprint. Fossils help scientists learn how life and environments have changed.

topics.title: Acceleration
topics.desc: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. An object accelerates if it speeds up, slows down, or changes direction. In everyday use people often say acceleration only for speeding up, but in physics all of those changes count.

topics.title: Kinetic and potential energy
topics.desc: Kinetic energy is the energy of motion. Potential energy is stored energy because of position or condition, such as a bike at the top of a hill or a stretched spring. Energy can change from one form to the other, like a ball slowing as it rolls uphill and speeding up as it comes down.

topics.title: Simple circuits
topics.desc: A simple electric circuit is a closed loop that lets current flow from a power source through a load, such as a bulb, and back again. If the loop is broken, the current stops. A switch opens or closes the loop, and wires need a complete path of conductive material.

topics.title: Electrical conductors
topics.desc: An electrical conductor lets electric current flow easily. Metals such as copper and aluminum are common conductors and are used in wires. An electrical insulator, such as rubber, glass or many plastics, resists current and is used to coat wires for safety.

topics.title: The greenhouse effect
topics.desc: The greenhouse effect is the way some gases in the atmosphere, including carbon dioxide and water vapor, absorb heat and keep Earth warmer than it would be without them. A stronger greenhouse effect from extra greenhouse gases traps more heat and raises global average temperatures.

topics.title: Renewable energy
topics.desc: Renewable energy comes from sources that are naturally replenished, such as sunlight, wind, moving water and geothermal heat. Fossil fuels like coal, oil and natural gas form much more slowly than we use them. Renewable sources still have costs, land use and other tradeoffs, but they do not run out in the same way.

topics.title: Recycling
topics.desc: Recycling turns used materials into new products instead of throwing them away. Rinse containers, follow your local rules, and keep items loose rather than bagged unless your collector says otherwise. Not everything with a recycling symbol is accepted curbside, so check the local list.

topics.title: The atmosphere
topics.desc: Earth’s atmosphere is the layer of gases around the planet. It is mostly nitrogen and oxygen, with smaller amounts of argon, carbon dioxide and other gases. It provides air to breathe, helps protect the surface from much of the Sun’s harmful radiation, and is where weather happens.

topics.title: Microscopes
topics.desc: A microscope magnifies things that are too small to see clearly with your eyes alone. A compound light microscope uses lenses and light; start on the lowest power, use the coarse knob to find the specimen, then sharpen with the fine knob. Keep slides thin and never use the coarse knob on high power.

topics.title: The human heart
topics.desc: The heart is a muscle that pumps blood through the body. The right side sends blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen. The left side sends oxygen-rich blood to the rest of the body. Valves keep blood moving in one direction.

topics.title: The lungs
topics.desc: The lungs are where oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves it. When you inhale, air travels down the windpipe to smaller airways and into tiny air sacs called alveoli. Oxygen crosses into the blood there, and carbon dioxide crosses out to be exhaled.

topics.title: Digestion
topics.desc: Digestion breaks food into nutrients the body can absorb. It starts in the mouth with chewing and saliva, continues in the stomach, and most nutrient absorption happens in the small intestine. The large intestine absorbs water and forms leftover material into stool.

topics.title: The American Revolution
topics.desc: The American Revolution was the war in which the 13 colonies broke away from Britain and became the United States. Fighting began in 1775 and ended with the Treaty of Paris in 1783, which recognized American independence.

topics.title: The Declaration of Independence
topics.desc: The Declaration of Independence, adopted on July 4, 1776, announced that the 13 colonies were separating from Britain. It says that people have rights such as life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness, and it lists complaints against the British king. Thomas Jefferson was its main author.

topics.title: The U.S. Constitution
topics.desc: The U.S. Constitution is the supreme law of the United States. Written in 1787, it sets up the national government, divides power among branches and states, and describes the rights of the people, including later amendments.

topics.title: The three branches of government
topics.desc: The U.S. federal government has three branches. Congress, the legislative branch, makes laws. The president and the executive branch carry out laws. The courts, the judicial branch, interpret laws and the Constitution.

topics.title: How a bill becomes a law
topics.desc: A bill is introduced in the House or Senate, studied in committee, and must pass both chambers in the same form. The president can sign it into law or veto it. Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote in both the House and the Senate.

topics.title: The Bill of Rights
topics.desc: The Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution, ratified in 1791. It protects freedoms such as speech, religion, the press, assembly and petition, and it also covers rights such as a jury trial and protection from unreasonable searches.

topics.title: Voting in the United States
topics.desc: In the United States, citizens who are 18 or older can vote once they meet their state's registration rules. People vote in local, state and federal elections. Rules about registration, ID and early or mail voting vary by state, so check your state or local election office.

topics.title: The Electoral College
topics.desc: The Electoral College is the system used to elect the U.S. president. There are 538 electors, and a candidate needs at least 270 electoral votes to win. Each state's electors usually equal its members of Congress. In most states, the candidate who wins the statewide popular vote gets all of that state's electors.

topics.title: The Civil War
topics.desc: The American Civil War was fought from 1861 to 1865 between the Union and the Confederate states that had seceded. Slavery and its expansion were at the center of the conflict. The Union won, and the 13th Amendment abolished slavery in the United States.

topics.title: The civil rights movement
topics.desc: The civil rights movement of the 1950s and 1960s was a struggle to end legal racial segregation and protect equal rights for Black Americans. It included court cases, boycotts, sit-ins, marches and new laws such as the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

topics.title: World War I
topics.desc: World War I lasted from 1914 to 1918 and was fought mainly in Europe between the Allied Powers and the Central Powers. The United States entered in 1917 on the Allied side. An armistice on November 11, 1918, ended the fighting.

topics.title: World War II
topics.desc: World War II lasted from 1939 to 1945 and was fought between the Allies and the Axis powers, including Nazi Germany, Italy and Japan. The United States entered after Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941. The war in Europe ended in May 1945, and Japan surrendered in September 1945.

topics.title: The Industrial Revolution
topics.desc: The Industrial Revolution was a period when many goods began to be made by machines in factories instead of by hand. It began in Britain in the 1700s and spread to other countries. Steam power, new machines and later electricity changed work, cities and transportation.

topics.title: Ancient Egypt
topics.desc: Ancient Egypt was a civilization along the Nile River in northeast Africa. It is known for pharaohs, pyramids, hieroglyphic writing and a religion that included many gods and a strong focus on the afterlife. The Nile's yearly flooding helped farming in a desert region.

topics.title: Ancient Rome
topics.desc: Ancient Rome began as a city in Italy, became a republic, and later an empire that controlled much of Europe, North Africa and the Middle East. Roman law, roads, Latin and republican ideas influenced later governments. The Western Roman Empire fell in 476 CE.

topics.title: Ancient Greece
topics.desc: Ancient Greece was made up of city-states such as Athens and Sparta, rather than one single country. Athens is known for an early form of democracy, and Greek thinkers, writers and athletes influenced later science, government, theater and the Olympic Games.

topics.title: The Silk Road
topics.desc: The Silk Road was a network of trade routes that linked East Asia with Central Asia, the Middle East and the Mediterranean for many centuries. Merchants traded goods such as silk, spices and metals, and the routes also spread ideas, technologies and religions.

topics.title: The Supreme Court
topics.desc: The Supreme Court is the highest court in the United States. It has nine justices who are nominated by the president and confirmed by the Senate, and they can serve for life. The Court interprets the Constitution and can strike down laws that conflict with it.

topics.title: Constitutional amendments
topics.desc: A constitutional amendment is a formal change to the U.S. Constitution. There are 27 amendments so far. The usual process is a two-thirds vote in both houses of Congress, then approval by three-fourths of the states.

topics.title: Checks and balances
topics.desc: Checks and balances are ways each branch of the U.S. government can limit the others so that one branch does not become too powerful. Examples include the president's veto, Congress overriding a veto, the Senate confirming appointments, and the courts reviewing laws.

topics.title: The Great Depression
topics.desc: The Great Depression was a severe worldwide economic downturn that began in the United States after the stock market crash of 1929. Many people lost jobs, homes and savings. In the U.S., President Franklin D. Roosevelt's New Deal created programs to provide relief and reform the financial system.

topics.title: The moon landing
topics.desc: On July 20, 1969, NASA's Apollo 11 mission landed the first humans on the Moon. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the lunar surface while Michael Collins stayed in orbit in the command module. Armstrong's first words included, "That's one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind."

topics.title: Metaphor and simile
topics.desc: A simile compares two things using like or as, such as "the cloud was like a cotton ball." A metaphor says one thing is another to make a comparison, such as "the cloud was a cotton ball." Both are figures of speech, but only a simile uses like or as.

topics.title: Plot
topics.desc: Plot is the sequence of events in a story. Many stories move from exposition, where the setup is introduced, through rising action and a climax, then falling action and a resolution. The conflict, the main problem the characters face, drives the plot forward.

topics.title: Irony
topics.desc: Irony is when the result or meaning is the opposite of what was expected or said. Verbal irony is saying one thing and meaning another. Situational irony is when events turn out the opposite of what you would expect. Dramatic irony is when the audience knows something a character does not.

topics.title: MLA citations
topics.desc: MLA style is often used in English and the humanities. A typical in-text citation is the author's last name and a page number in parentheses, such as (Lopez 12). At the end, a Works Cited list gives full details so a reader can find each source.

topics.title: APA citations
topics.desc: APA style is often used in the social sciences. A typical in-text citation is the author's last name and the year, such as (Lopez, 2023). At the end, a References list gives full details for each source. Page numbers are added when you quote a specific passage.

topics.title: Test-taking strategies
topics.desc: Read the directions and skim the test so you can budget your time. Answer the questions you know first, then return to harder ones. For multiple choice, try to think of the answer before looking at the options, and cross out choices you know are wrong. Check your work if time remains.

topics.title: Making a study schedule
topics.desc: List upcoming due dates and exams, then break each subject into short study sessions across several days instead of one long cram. Put the hardest or earliest work first, include breaks, and leave a little buffer for things that take longer than expected.

topics.title: Annotating a text
topics.desc: Annotating means marking a text as you read to help you understand it. Underline key claims, circle words to look up, and write short notes or questions in the margin. Mark only the most useful parts so the page stays readable.

topics.title: Writing an essay outline
topics.desc: An outline is a plan for your essay. Start with your thesis, then list each body paragraph's main point and the evidence you will use. Add a note for the introduction and conclusion. A clear outline makes the draft faster and helps you stay on topic.

topics.title: Introductions and conclusions
topics.desc: An introduction should present the topic and end with your thesis, the main claim the essay will support. A conclusion should not just copy the introduction. It should tie the points together and leave the reader with the significance of your argument, without adding a major new claim.

topics.title: Avoiding plagiarism
topics.desc: Plagiarism is presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own. Put borrowed wording in quotation marks, cite the source, and paraphrase in your own words instead of only swapping a few terms. When you are unsure, cite. Your school's policy explains the rules and consequences.

topics.title: Do Not Disturb
topics.desc: Do Not Disturb, or Focus modes on iPhone, can silence calls, alerts and notifications so you can sleep or work. You can usually allow repeated calls or notifications from chosen people. Check that it turns off when you want, or set a schedule so it does not stay on by accident.

topics.title: AirDrop
topics.desc: AirDrop is Apple's way to send photos, files and links between nearby Apple devices over Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, without using a cable. Set AirDrop to receive from Everyone for a few minutes or only from Contacts, then turn it back if you do not want requests from strangers.

topics.title: iCloud
topics.desc: iCloud is Apple's cloud service for backing up an iPhone and syncing photos, files and settings across your Apple devices. A backup can help you restore a new or reset phone. Photos and files in iCloud count toward your storage plan, so check Settings if you run out of space.

topics.title: Low Power Mode
topics.desc: Low Power Mode on iPhone reduces background activity and some visual effects to make the remaining battery last longer. Your phone may fetch mail less often and dim features until you charge it or turn the mode off. It is useful when you cannot charge soon, not as an everyday setting for everyone.

topics.title: Find My
topics.desc: Find My can help you locate a missing iPhone, iPad, Mac or AirTag on a map, play a sound, or mark the device as lost. It works best when the device is powered on and connected, and when Find My was already turned on. A lost mode can lock the device and show a message with a contact number.

topics.title: Offloading apps
topics.desc: Offloading an app removes the app from your phone but keeps its documents and data. You get the storage back that the app itself used, and you can reinstall it later without starting all over. Deleting an app can also remove its data, so offload if you think you will need that data again.

topics.title: Screen Time
topics.desc: Screen Time on iPhone shows how long you use apps and can set limits, downtime or a passcode so a younger user cannot just change the rules. Use it to see where time goes and to set limits you actually want, and keep the passcode different from your device passcode if you are setting limits for yourself.

topics.title: Restarting a frozen phone
topics.desc: If an iPhone is frozen, first try a regular restart: press and hold a volume button and the side button, then slide to power off, wait, and turn it back on. If the screen will not respond, use a force restart: quickly press volume up, then volume down, then hold the side button until the Apple logo appears.

topics.title: Freeing phone storage
topics.desc: On iPhone, open Settings, then General, then iPhone Storage to see what is using space. Large videos, downloaded files and unused apps are common. Offload unused apps, delete videos you already backed up, and clear downloads in Safari or Files. Restart after large deletions if the free space has not updated yet.

topics.title: Mobile hotspots
topics.desc: A mobile hotspot lets other devices use your phone's cellular data as Wi-Fi. It can use up data quickly and drain the battery, and some plans charge extra or cap hotspot data. Use a password, turn the hotspot off when you are done, and avoid it if you are low on data.

topics.title: Screen mirroring
topics.desc: Screen mirroring shows your phone or computer display on a TV or monitor. AirPlay works with Apple devices and many compatible TVs, and some TVs or apps also support Chromecast or an HDMI cable. Both devices usually need to be on the same Wi-Fi network, except when you use a cable.

topics.title: USB-C and Lightning
topics.desc: Lightning is Apple's older small charging connector used on many earlier iPhones. USB-C is a wider, reversible connector now used on newer iPhones, many Android phones, laptops and chargers. A cable has to match the ports on both ends, and charging speed also depends on the charger, not only the plug shape.

topics.title: Strong passwords
topics.desc: A strong password is long, unique to that account, and hard to guess. A passphrase of several unrelated words is easier to remember than a short mix of characters. Use a different password for email and banking, and a password manager can store them so you do not reuse the same one everywhere.

topics.title: Two-factor authentication
topics.desc: Two-factor authentication, or 2FA, asks for a second check after your password, such as a code from a text message or an authenticator app. It makes it much harder for someone who only has your password to get in. Keep backup codes in a safe place in case you lose your phone.

topics.title: Phishing messages
topics.desc: A phishing message tries to trick you into sharing a password, code or payment, often by posing as a bank, school, store or delivery service. Check the real address, not just the display name, and do not tap unexpected links or share a login code. If you are unsure, open the official app or website yourself.

topics.title: Private browsing
topics.desc: Private or Incognito browsing does not save your history, cookies or form entries on that device after you close the window. It does not make you invisible. Your school, workplace, internet provider or the sites you visit can still see activity, and downloads you save stay on the device.

topics.title: Browser cookies
topics.desc: Cookies are small files a site stores in your browser to remember things such as a login, language or items in a cart. Some cookies also track visits across sites for advertising. You can usually block or clear cookies in browser settings, but you may have to log in again afterward.

topics.title: VPNs
topics.desc: A VPN, or virtual private network, sends your internet traffic through an encrypted tunnel to a server, which can hide it from a local Wi-Fi network. It does not make you fully anonymous, and a poorly chosen VPN can see or mishandle your traffic. A VPN also will not fix a device that already has malware.

topics.title: Software updates
topics.desc: Software updates fix bugs and close security holes, and they sometimes add features. Install updates from the official Settings app or app store, not from a random pop-up or text. Keep your phone plugged in or well charged, and back it up first if the update is a large system version.

topics.title: Public Wi-Fi safety
topics.desc: Public Wi-Fi in cafes, airports and hotels is convenient but easier for others on the network to snoop if a site is not secure. Avoid logging into banking or entering passwords on unknown networks when you can use your phone's cellular data or a trusted VPN instead. Confirm you joined the official network, not a similarly named fake one.

topics.title: Cloud storage
topics.desc: Cloud storage keeps files on a company's servers so you can open them from other devices, such as iCloud, Google Drive or OneDrive. Your files are only as safe as your account, so use a strong unique password and two-factor authentication. Check whether a file is stored only in the cloud, only on the device, or both.

topics.title: Email attachments
topics.desc: Open attachments only when you expect the file and trust the sender. Check the real email address and the file type; unexpected .exe, .zip or unusual documents can carry malware. If a message looks odd, contact the person through a number or account you already have instead of opening the file.

topics.title: Digital footprints
topics.desc: A digital footprint is the trail of information you leave online, including posts, photos, comments, accounts and data collected about you. Even deleted posts can be saved or shared by others. Search your name occasionally, tighten privacy settings, and think twice before posting something you would not want a school or employer to see.

topics.title: Social app privacy
topics.desc: In a social app's privacy settings, choose who can see your posts, story and location, and who can message or tag you. Turn off location sharing when you do not need it, and review tagged photos. A public account can be seen by anyone, including people you do not know.

topics.title: Blocking a number
topics.desc: Blocking a number stops calls and texts from that number from ringing through on most phones. On iPhone, open the call or thread, tap the info button, and choose Block this Caller. Blocked messages may still be stored in a filtered list, and a person can try a different number, so also report harassment if it continues.

topics.title: Backing up a phone
topics.desc: A backup is a copy of your apps, photos, settings and data that you can use if the phone is lost, broken or reset. On iPhone you can back up with iCloud or a computer. Back up before a major update or trade-in, and check that recent photos actually appear in the backup or photo library.

topics.title: App permissions
topics.desc: App permissions are the kinds of access an app asks for, such as the camera, microphone, photos, location or contacts. Grant only what the app needs for a feature you actually use. You can change permissions later in Settings, and you can often choose While Using the App instead of Always for location.

topics.title: Clearing a browser cache
topics.desc: A browser cache stores pieces of websites so pages can load faster next time. Clearing the cache can fix a page that looks stuck or outdated, but you may need to log in again and pages may load more slowly at first. In Safari on iPhone, you can clear history and website data in Settings.

topics.title: Pairing a Bluetooth device
topics.desc: To pair headphones or a speaker, put the device in pairing mode, open Bluetooth in Settings, and tap the device's name. Stay close during setup, and type a PIN if asked, often 0000 or 1234 if a manual does not give another code. Forget the device in Settings if it will not reconnect, then pair it again.

topics.title: If a phone gets wet
topics.desc: If a phone gets wet, take it out of the water, power it off if it is on, and do not charge it or plug anything in. Dry the outside with a cloth and let it dry in a warm, dry place. Skip a bag of rice, which can leave dust and does not dry the inside well. If it was in dirty or salt water, or it will not turn on later, get professional help.

topics.title: Dark mode
topics.desc: Dark mode uses a darker background that some people find easier on the eyes in low light and that can save a little battery on phones with OLED screens. It does not automatically make every app easier to read. You can schedule it in Settings or switch it in Control Center.

topics.title: Muting a group chat
topics.desc: Muting a group chat keeps the conversation but stops most notifications, so your phone is not buzzing all day. On iPhone, open the thread, tap the group name or info button, and turn on Hide Alerts. You can still open the chat when you want to catch up.

topics.title: Washing your hands
topics.desc: Wash your hands with soap and water for about 20 seconds, including the backs, between the fingers and under the nails, then rinse and dry. Do this before eating, after using the bathroom, and after coughing or handling shared surfaces. Use hand sanitizer with at least 60 percent alcohol when soap and water are not available, but wash with soap if hands are visibly dirty.

topics.title: Getting enough sleep
topics.desc: Most teenagers need about 8 to 10 hours of sleep, and most adults need about 7 or more. A regular bedtime, a darker quieter room, and putting screens away before bed can help. If you often cannot sleep, snore loudly, or feel exhausted every day, talk with a parent, school nurse or doctor.

topics.title: Drinking enough water
topics.desc: Your body needs water throughout the day, and thirst is a useful signal. A rough guide is pale yellow urine; very dark urine can mean you need more fluids. You usually need more water in heat or during exercise. If a doctor has given you fluid limits, follow that advice instead of general tips.

topics.title: Stretching
topics.desc: Stretching can help you move more comfortably, especially after a short warm-up when muscles are less cold. Move into a stretch gently, breathe, and hold it without bouncing or pushing into sharp pain. If you have an injury, follow a coach or clinician's advice instead of forcing a stretch.

topics.title: Sunscreen
topics.desc: Sunscreen helps protect skin from the sun's ultraviolet rays, which can cause sunburn and raise long-term skin cancer risk. Use a broad-spectrum sunscreen of at least SPF 30, apply it before you go out, and reapply after swimming, sweating or a couple of hours outdoors. Sunscreen is one part of sun safety, along with shade, clothing and sunglasses.

topics.title: Cleaning a small cut
topics.desc: For a small cut, wash your hands, then rinse the wound with clean water and gently clean around it. Use light pressure with a clean cloth if it is bleeding, then add a bandage. Skip harsh cleaners in the wound unless a clinician tells you to use them. Get medical care if bleeding will not stop, the cut is deep or dirty, or you have not had needed tetanus shots.

topics.title: Treating a minor burn
topics.desc: For a small heat burn, cool the area under cool running water for about 10 to 20 minutes. Do not use ice, butter or toothpaste. You can cover it loosely with a clean bandage after cooling. Get medical care for burns that are large, deep, blistered over a wide area, on the face, hands, feet or joints, or if you are not sure it is minor.

topics.title: Choking first aid
topics.desc: If someone is choking and cannot cough, speak or breathe, call emergency services right away and ask someone to get help. For a conscious adult or older child, trained first aid uses back blows and abdominal thrusts to try to clear the airway. This is not a substitute for a first-aid class, and the steps differ for infants and for someone who becomes unresponsive.

topics.title: When to call 911
topics.desc: Call 911 in the United States for a medical, fire or safety emergency that needs help right away, such as trouble breathing, chest pain, a serious injury, a seizure that will not stop, a fire, or a crime in progress. Stay as calm as you can, give the location, and follow the dispatcher's instructions. If you are not sure it is an emergency, it is still reasonable to call.

topics.title: RICE for a sprain
topics.desc: RICE stands for rest, ice, compression and elevation, a common first step for a mild sprain. Rest the joint, apply a cold pack wrapped in a cloth for short periods, use a wrap if you have been shown how, and keep the area raised. See a doctor or athletic trainer if you cannot bear weight, the joint looks deformed, or pain and swelling are severe or not improving.

topics.title: Screen eye strain
topics.desc: Long screen time can make eyes feel dry, tired or sore. Try the 20-20-20 idea: about every 20 minutes, look at something about 20 feet away for 20 seconds, blink often, and raise the brightness so you are not squinting. If headaches or vision changes keep happening, get your eyes checked.

topics.title: Good posture
topics.desc: Good posture means sitting or standing so your ears, shoulders and hips line up reasonably well, with your back supported and both feet on the floor when you sit. Keep screens at about eye level so you are not craning your neck down. Change positions and stand up sometimes; no single pose is meant to be held all day.

topics.title: Warming up before exercise
topics.desc: A warm-up raises your heart rate gently and moves the muscles you are about to use, such as a few minutes of brisk walking or light versions of the activity. It can make exercise feel easier and may lower injury risk compared with starting at full speed while cold. Save long, deep stretches for after the body is already warm, unless a coach has given you a different plan.

topics.title: Reading a nutrition label
topics.desc: A Nutrition Facts label shows serving size first, then calories and nutrients in one serving. If you eat two servings, double the numbers. The percent daily value is a rough guide based on a typical 2,000-calorie diet, not a personal target for every person. Use the ingredients list if you need to avoid a specific allergen.

topics.title: Food allergies
topics.desc: A food allergy is an immune system reaction that can be mild or life-threatening. Common allergens include peanuts, tree nuts, milk, eggs, soy, wheat, fish and sesame, but any food can be a problem for someone. An intolerance is usually uncomfortable but is not the same as an allergy. Take a diagnosed allergy seriously, read labels, and follow a doctor's emergency plan, including epinephrine if it was prescribed.

topics.title: Caffeine
topics.desc: Caffeine is a stimulant in coffee, tea, many sodas and energy drinks. It can help you feel more alert, but too much can cause jitters, a fast heartbeat or trouble sleeping, especially later in the day. Energy drinks can be very high in caffeine. If caffeine makes you unwell or you have a heart condition, ask a doctor what is safe for you.

topics.title: Talking about stress
topics.desc: Stress is your body's response to pressure, and it helps to talk with a parent, counselor, coach or another trusted adult instead of keeping it all in. Short-term tools include sleep, movement, taking a break, and slow breathing. If stress or sadness lasts, or you have thoughts of hurting yourself, tell an adult right away or call or text 988 in the United States for the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline.

topics.title: Brushing and flossing
topics.desc: Brush your teeth twice a day with fluoride toothpaste and clean between your teeth once a day with floss or another interdental cleaner. Brush gently along the gumline rather than scrubbing hard. Regular dental checkups help catch problems early, and a dentist can show you a technique that fits your teeth.

topics.title: Concussion warning signs
topics.desc: A concussion is a brain injury from a blow or jolt to the head or body. Warning signs include headache, confusion, nausea, dizziness, balance problems, unusual sleepiness, or acting different from usual. Stop playing and see a medical professional. Returning to sports the same day is unsafe, even if you feel better quickly.

topics.title: Cooling down after exercise
topics.desc: A cool-down is a few minutes of easier movement after a hard workout, such as a slow jog or walk, so your heart rate can come down gradually. It is a good time for gentle stretching while muscles are still warm. Stop and get help if you feel chest pain, faint, or severely short of breath.

topics.title: Making a budget
topics.desc: A budget is a plan for your money. List your income, then list needed expenses such as food, transportation and bills, then savings, then wants. If spending is higher than income, cut wants first or look for more income. Checking it weekly helps you catch problems early.

topics.title: Saving money
topics.desc: Saving means setting money aside for later instead of spending all of it now. Paying yourself first, even a small amount from each paycheck or allowance, adds up. Keep savings in a separate account if you can, and pick a goal, such as an emergency fund or a purchase, so the money has a purpose.

topics.title: Checking and savings accounts
topics.desc: A checking account is meant for everyday spending with a debit card or transfers. A savings account is meant to hold money you do not plan to spend right away and may pay a little interest. Some banks limit certain savings transfers, and both accounts can have fees, so read the account terms.

topics.title: Interest
topics.desc: Interest is the cost of borrowing money or the money you earn for keeping money in some accounts. If you borrow, you usually pay back the amount plus interest. If a savings account pays interest, the bank pays you a percentage. A higher rate helps you more when you save and costs you more when you borrow.

topics.title: Debit versus credit cards
topics.desc: A debit card spends money that is already in your checking account. A credit card borrows money you have to pay back, often with interest if you do not pay the full bill on time. A credit card can help build a credit history if used carefully, but carrying a balance can get expensive. Treat both as real money.

topics.title: Credit scores
topics.desc: A credit score is a number lenders use to estimate how reliably you have repaid borrowed money. Paying bills on time and keeping credit card balances low usually helps. You generally need a credit account in your name, such as a card or loan, before a score is created. Checking your own score does not hurt it.

topics.title: Pay stubs
topics.desc: A pay stub is the record that comes with a paycheck. It shows gross pay, then deductions such as taxes and benefits, and the net pay you actually receive. Check the hours, pay rate and deductions so you can catch mistakes. Keep stubs for your records, especially at tax time.

topics.title: Sales tax
topics.desc: Sales tax is a tax added to many purchases, set by the state or local government. The register total can be higher than the shelf price because tax is added at checkout. Rates and which items are taxed vary by place, so the same product can cost a little more in one city than another.

topics.title: Compound interest
topics.desc: Compound interest is interest earned on both the original amount and the interest already added. In savings, that can help money grow faster over time. On a credit card or loan, it can make a balance grow if you pay only a little and interest keeps being added. Time and the interest rate both matter a lot.

topics.title: Needs versus wants
topics.desc: Needs are things you must have or that would cause real harm to go without, such as food, housing, medicine and essential transportation. Wants make life nicer but can wait, such as upgrades, snacks or extra subscriptions. When money is tight, cover needs and a little savings first, then decide which wants are worth it.

topics.title: Emergency funds
topics.desc: An emergency fund is money set aside for unexpected costs, such as a broken phone, a car repair or a lost shift, so you do not have to borrow right away. Start small if needed and keep it in a savings account you can reach without a penalty. Use it for true surprises, then build it back up.

topics.title: Avoiding money scams
topics.desc: A money scam tries to get you to send cash, gift cards, crypto or account codes, often by pretending to be a company, a crush, a prize or someone in trouble. Pause if someone rushes you or asks you to keep it secret. Do not send money or codes to someone you have not verified, and check a company's real number or website yourself.

topics.title: Direct deposit
topics.desc: Direct deposit sends your paycheck electronically into your bank account instead of giving you a paper check. Your employer needs your routing number and account number, which are on a check or in your banking app. Check the first deposit to confirm the amount and the account are correct, and tell your employer if you change banks.

topics.title: Hourly pay versus salary
topics.desc: Hourly pay is a set amount for each hour you work, and overtime rules may apply if you work extra hours. A salary is a fixed amount for a pay period, often quoted as a yearly figure, even if some weeks are longer than others. Compare offers by estimating total pay, benefits and expected hours, not only the headline number.

topics.title: Writing a resume
topics.desc: A resume is a short summary of your work, school, skills and activities for a job or program. Put your name and contact info at the top, then education, experience and skills, using short bullet points that start with strong verbs and show what you did. Keep it to one page if you are early in your career, and tailor it to the role.

topics.title: Job interviews
topics.desc: A job interview is a conversation to see if you and the role are a good fit. Read the job post, prepare a few examples of work or school you have done, and be ready to ask one or two questions about the job. Arrive a little early, listen carefully, and send a short thank-you message afterward.

topics.title: Tipping
topics.desc: Tipping is an extra payment for service, common in U.S. restaurants, hair salons and for delivery. Many people tip about 15 to 20 percent of the pre-tax bill for table service when the service was fine. Check the receipt; some places already add a service charge. Rules differ by country, so look it up when you travel.

topics.title: Opening a bank account
topics.desc: To open a checking or savings account, a bank or credit union usually asks for photo ID, your Social Security number or ITIN if you have one, and a small opening deposit. Compare fees, overdraft rules and whether you need a parent or guardian as a joint owner if you are under 18. Read the account agreement before you sign.

topics.title: Gross versus net pay
topics.desc: Gross pay is what you earn before deductions. Net pay, or take-home pay, is what you actually receive after taxes and other deductions such as health insurance. Compare job offers by looking at both the pay rate and what is taken out, not only the headline wage.

topics.title: Kitchen knife basics
topics.desc: Keep fingers curled under on the hand that holds the food, and cut with a claw grip so fingertips stay back from the blade. Use a stable board, don't try to catch a falling knife, and wash knives carefully by hand or as the maker directs. A sharp knife is easier to control than a dull one.

topics.title: Boiling versus simmering
topics.desc: Boiling means the liquid is at 212°F (100°C) at sea level, with large, rolling bubbles. Simmering is gentler, with small bubbles that rise slowly, usually just below a boil. Use a boil for pasta or reducing a liquid quickly, and a simmer for soups, sauces and tougher cuts of food that need steady, gentle heat.

topics.title: Sautéing
topics.desc: Sautéing is cooking food quickly in a little oil or butter over medium-high heat, usually in a wide pan. Heat the pan first, don't crowd the food so it browns instead of steaming, and stir or toss as it cooks. Cut pieces to a similar size so they finish at the same time.

topics.title: Baking versus roasting
topics.desc: Baking and roasting both use dry oven heat. People usually say baking for breads, cakes and other batters, and roasting for meats and vegetables, often at a higher temperature so the outside browns. Follow the recipe temperature and use the rack position it calls for.

topics.title: Scrambling eggs
topics.desc: Beat the eggs with a pinch of salt. Warm a little butter or oil in a nonstick pan over medium-low heat, pour in the eggs, and stir gently as they set. Take them off the heat while they still look slightly moist; they keep cooking in the pan.

topics.title: Boiling eggs
topics.desc: Place eggs in a saucepan and cover them with an inch of cold water. Bring to a boil, then turn off the heat, cover, and let sit: about 6 to 8 minutes for a jammy yolk, or 10 to 12 minutes for a firm hard-boiled yolk. Move the eggs to cold water so they stop cooking and are easier to peel.

topics.title: Food safety temperatures
topics.desc: Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) and ground beef to 160°F (71°C). Steaks and chops are often considered safe at 145°F (63°C) with a short rest, and leftovers should be reheated to 165°F. Use a food thermometer in the thickest part, not just color, and keep cold food at or below 40°F (4°C).

topics.title: Storing leftovers
topics.desc: Cool leftovers and refrigerate them within two hours, or within one hour if the food has been in a hot room. Use shallow containers so they cool faster, eat or freeze them within a few days, and reheat until steaming hot. When in doubt, throw it out rather than risk leftover food that smells or looks off.

topics.title: Defrosting food safely
topics.desc: The safest ways to thaw food are in the refrigerator, under cold running water, or in the microwave if you will cook it right away. Do not thaw meat or poultry on the counter at room temperature, where the outside can sit in the danger zone while the inside is still frozen. Cook food thawed in the microwave immediately.

topics.title: Preventing cross-contamination
topics.desc: Cross-contamination is when germs from raw meat, poultry or seafood get onto ready-to-eat food. Use separate cutting boards or wash the board, knife and hands with hot soapy water after cutting raw meat. Keep raw meat on a plate on the bottom fridge shelf so juices cannot drip onto other food.

topics.title: Best-by and use-by dates
topics.desc: A use-by or expiration date is about safety for some foods, especially infant formula, and you should follow it. A best-by or best-before date is usually about quality, not an automatic deadline; many foods are still fine if they were stored well and show no spoilage. When a food looks, smells or feels wrong, do not eat it even if the date has not passed.

topics.title: Making oatmeal
topics.desc: For stovetop oats, use about 2 cups of water or milk per 1 cup of rolled oats, a pinch of salt, and simmer, stirring, until thick and creamy, often 5 minutes. Quick oats cook faster; steel-cut oats take longer and need more liquid. Sweeten or add fruit after cooking if you want.

topics.title: Making pancakes
topics.desc: Mix the dry ingredients, then the wet, and stir just until combined; a few lumps are fine and help keep pancakes tender. Cook on a greased medium pan until bubbles form and the edges look set, then flip once and cook the other side. Keep the heat moderate so the inside cooks before the outside burns.

topics.title: Making a grilled cheese
topics.desc: Butter the outside of two bread slices, add cheese between them, and cook in a skillet over medium-low heat until the bread is golden and the cheese has melted, flipping once. Covering the pan for a minute can help the cheese melt without burning the bread.

topics.title: Making a quesadilla
topics.desc: Scatter cheese and any fillings on one half of a tortilla, fold it over, and cook in a lightly oiled skillet over medium heat until both sides are golden and the cheese melts. Let it sit a minute before cutting so the filling doesn't slide out.

topics.title: Salting pasta water
topics.desc: Salt the water after it is boiling, just before you add the pasta. The pasta absorbs some of that seasoning as it cooks, so the finished dish tastes better than if you only salt the sauce. A common starting point is about 1 tablespoon of kosher salt per 4 quarts of water, then adjust to your taste and any doctor's advice on sodium.

topics.title: Microwave safety
topics.desc: Use microwave-safe glass or labeled plastic, not metal or foil, which can spark. Watch out for steam when you uncover a hot container, and stir food so it heats evenly. Superheated water can erupt, so use a microwave-safe container and care when heating plain water. If a dish says do not microwave, follow that.

topics.title: Grease fires
topics.desc: If oil in a pan catches fire, turn off the heat if you can do it safely and slide a metal lid over the pan to smother the flames. Never pour water on a grease fire; it can explode the fire outward. Baking soda can help on a small pan fire. If the fire is spreading, leave, close the door, and call 911.

topics.title: American football downs
topics.desc: A down is one play. The offense has four downs to gain 10 yards. If they succeed, they get a new set of downs. If they don't, the other team usually takes over. Teams often punt or try a field goal on fourth down instead of risking a turnover on downs.

topics.title: Touchdowns and field goals
topics.desc: A touchdown is worth 6 points when the ball is carried or caught in the opponent's end zone. The team can then try an extra point kick (1) or a two-point conversion. A field goal is normally 3 points, kicked through the goalposts, often on fourth down or at the end of a half.

topics.title: Baseball strikes and innings
topics.desc: A strike is a pitch in the strike zone that the batter does not hit fairly, or a swing and a miss, or a foul (except a foul cannot be strike three unless it is a bunt). Three strikes make an out. An inning is a turn for both teams to bat; a regulation game is usually nine innings.

topics.title: Golf scoring
topics.desc: In stroke play, the person with the fewest total shots wins. Par is the expected number of strokes for a hole. A birdie is one under par, an eagle is two under, and a bogey is one over par. Lower totals are better.

topics.title: Freestyle swimming
topics.desc: Freestyle usually means the front crawl: alternate arm strokes, a flutter kick, and breathing to the side. Keep your body fairly long and level, and turn your head to breathe rather than lifting it straight up. In a freestyle event you may use any stroke, but crawl is the fastest for most people.

topics.title: Basketball layups
topics.desc: A layup is a close-range shot off the backboard while moving toward the hoop. Dribble in, pick up the ball, and jump off the opposite foot from the shooting hand: right-hand layup, jump off the left foot. Use the backboard square as a target, and protect the ball with your body.

topics.title: Chess check and checkmate
topics.desc: Check means your king is under attack and you must get out of it by moving the king, blocking the attack, or capturing the attacking piece. Checkmate means the king is in check and there is no legal way out, so the game is over and that player loses. You cannot make a move that leaves your own king in check.

topics.title: Castling
topics.desc: Castling is a special king-and-rook move: the king moves two squares toward a rook, and that rook jumps to the square the king crossed. You can castle only if neither piece has moved, the squares between them are empty, and the king is not in check and does not pass through or land on an attacked square.

topics.title: Sudoku
topics.desc: Sudoku is a puzzle on a 9-by-9 grid divided into 3-by-3 boxes. Fill every row, column and box with the digits 1 through 9, each used once. Start with cells that have the fewest possibilities, pencil in candidates, and never guess if a logical next number is available.

topics.title: Uno
topics.desc: In Uno, you take turns playing a card that matches the color or number (or symbol) of the card on the pile, or you play a wild. Draw if you cannot play. Action cards can skip, reverse, or make the next player draw. Say “Uno” when you have one card left, or you may have to draw if someone catches you.

topics.title: In-game purchases
topics.desc: In-game purchases are optional items, currency or passes you buy with real money inside a game. Set a password, use purchase approvals, and check platform spending limits so a game cannot charge you by accident. Treat leftover currency as money already spent, and don't feel you have to buy an advantage to play.

topics.title: Checking tire pressure
topics.desc: Look up the recommended PSI on the driver's door sticker, not only the tire sidewall, which shows the maximum. Check when the tires are cold, unscrew the valve cap, press a gauge on the valve, and add or release air until you hit the number. Recheck all four tires, and the spare if you have one.

topics.title: Pumping gas
topics.desc: Park at the pump, turn the car off, and open the fuel door. Choose the grade your owner's manual recommends, usually regular unless the car requires premium. Insert the nozzle fully, pump, then wait a moment, hang the nozzle up, and tighten the cap until it clicks if it is a click cap. Don't smoke or use your phone in a way that distracts you at the pump.

topics.title: Checking engine oil
topics.desc: Park on level ground, turn the engine off, and wait a few minutes. Pull out the dipstick, wipe it, put it back in fully, then pull it out again and read the level between the min and max marks. If it is low, add the oil type in your owner's manual a little at a time and recheck. A warning light or a very low level means you should not keep driving.

topics.title: Jump-starting a car
topics.desc: Only jump-start if both batteries are the same voltage, usually 12 volts, and you know the correct terminals. Connect the red clamp to the dead battery's positive terminal, then to the good battery's positive. Connect the black clamp to the good battery's negative, then to an unpainted metal ground on the dead car, not the dead negative terminal if the manual says not to. Start the good car, then the dead one, and remove the cables in reverse order. If you are unsure, call for roadside help.

topics.title: Changing a spare tire
topics.desc: Pull well off the road, turn on hazard lights, and set the parking brake. Loosen the lug nuts slightly before jacking, jack at the lift point in the owner's manual, remove the nuts, swap the wheel, snug the nuts, lower the car, then tighten the nuts in a star pattern. A donut spare is usually for short, slower trips to a shop, not highway speeds for long distances.

topics.title: Dashboard warning lights
topics.desc: A red oil, brake or temperature warning usually means you should stop safely as soon as you can and check the manual or get help. An amber check-engine or tire light often means something needs service soon, but not always an instant stop. Look up the exact symbol in your owner's manual instead of ignoring a light.

topics.title: Seat belts
topics.desc: A seat belt should sit across the hips and mid-chest, not the stomach or neck, and it should be snug. Everyone in the car should buckle up, including the back seat. A belt works with the airbag; sitting too close or leaving the belt off can make a crash much more dangerous.

topics.title: Car insurance basics
topics.desc: Car insurance helps pay for damage or injury after a crash, theft or other covered events, according to your policy. Liability coverage pays others if you are at fault; collision and comprehensive cover damage to your own car in different situations. State laws set minimums, and a deductible is what you pay first before the insurer pays the rest.

topics.title: Getting a learner's permit
topics.desc: A learner's permit lets you practice driving with restrictions before a full license. Rules vary by state, but you usually have to be a minimum age, pass a written knowledge test and an eye test, and complete an application with ID and, if you are a minor, a parent or guardian's consent. Drive only with the passengers and hours your state allows.

topics.title: Parallel parking
topics.desc: Line up with the car in front of the space, about two to three feet away. Reverse and turn toward the curb to enter the space, then straighten and turn the other way to tuck the bumper in. You should end up a reasonable distance from the curb, usually within about 12 inches in many tests, without hitting the cars around you. Practice in an empty lot first.

topics.title: Pedestrian safety
topics.desc: Cross at a corner or marked crosswalk when you can, look left, right, then left again, and make sure drivers have stopped before you step out. On a two-way street, watch for turning cars. At night, wear something visible, and stay off your phone while crossing. Drivers should yield, but do not assume they have seen you.

topics.title: Locking a bicycle
topics.desc: Lock the frame and if you can a wheel to a solid rack, using a sturdy U-lock or a quality heavy chain, not only a thin cable. Don't leave the lock near the ground where it is easier to attack, and take lights and loose bags with you. Register the bike and photograph the serial number in case it is stolen.

topics.title: Tying a necktie
topics.desc: For a common four-in-hand knot, drape the tie around your neck with the wide end hanging lower. Wrap the wide end across the narrow end, around the back, and across the front again, then up through the neck loop and down through the front knot. Slide the knot up and dimple the center if you want a neater look.

topics.title: Sewing on a button
topics.desc: Thread a needle and knot the end. From the back of the fabric, sew through each pair of buttonholes several times, leaving a tiny shank of thread under the button if the fabric is thick, then wrap the thread around that shank and knot it on the back. Match the thread color and don't pull so tight that the fabric puckers.

topics.title: Using a fire extinguisher
topics.desc: Use a fire extinguisher only if the fire is small, you have a clear exit, and you know what is burning. Remember PASS: pull the pin, aim at the base of the fire, squeeze the handle, and sweep from side to side. If the fire grows or the room fills with smoke, leave and call 911.

topics.title: Smoke alarms
topics.desc: Smoke alarms should be on every level of a home, inside bedrooms, and outside sleeping areas. Test them monthly, replace batteries when the unit chirps or as the maker directs, and replace the whole alarm when it reaches the date on the back, often after about 10 years. Never take the battery out just to stop a nuisance chirp without fixing the cause.

topics.title: Airport security basics
topics.desc: At U.S. airport security, have your ID and boarding pass ready, and follow the bin rules for shoes, laptops and liquids. Liquids in carry-on bags generally must be in containers of 3.4 ounces (100 ml) or less, in one quart-size bag, with exceptions such as medically necessary items you should declare. Put metal items in a bin, and wait for the officer's instructions.
